newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea issues more arrest warrants over Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea issues more arrest warrants over Hanbo.

text.p: A South Korean court issued arrest warrants on Tuesday for a close associate of President Kim Young-sam and a top ruling party official over a loan scandal surrounding the failed Hanbo Steel Co, court officials said.

The warrants were for Hong In-gil, a senior official at the presidential Blue House until a few months before he was elected to parliament last year, and Chung Jae-chull, highest ranked New Korea Party member after Kim and party chairman Lee Hong-koo.
They were issued only hours after prosecutors filed a request for warrants to arrest Hong and Chung on charges the two had taken kickbacks from Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo.

The tycoon has already been arrested on charges of fraud and other violations in connection with five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans the steelmaker piled up before it was declared insolvent on January 23.
Two leading local bankers have also been arrested.
"The deputies are charged with taking kickbacks from Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo," a prosecution official told Reuters.

He said Hong was accused of taking 800 million won on four occasions last year from the tycoon, who asked him to persuade banks to provide loans to Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate.
Lawmaker Chung was accused of accepting 100 million won from the Hanbo founder, who asked him to pressure bankers into offering loans, the official said.

He was also accused of passing on another 100 million won to opposition member of parliament Kwon Roh-kap from the tycoon who tried to silence criticism over the huge loans that exceeded the value of their collateral.
Hong and lawmaker Chung are the first politicians to be probed over the loan scandal that has shocked South Korea and put the heat on Kim in a presidential election year.
Kim, who last month ordered a probe into the loans, has called the scandal a typical example of corruption.

Prosecutors also questioned the Hanbo founder's driver on Tuesday on suspicions he carried apple crates stuffed with cash to bankers and politicians, senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog told reporters. "The driver is a very important person in our investigation," he said.
Hong denied taking money from Hanbo before he was summoned by prosecutors on Monday.
Kwon said he had nothing to do with Hanbo loans. But he has said he took between 150 million and 160 million won from Hanbo, partly to fund an election campaign.
The other lawmaker has not publicly commented.
Prosecutors have summoned Kwon, a top aide to Kim Dae-jung, who heads the main opposition National Congress for New Politics.
But the National Congress and a smaller opposition group, the United Liberal Democratic Party, on Tuesday urged him not to report to the prosecution office.

"The prosecutors are trying to implicate the opposition to whitewash the nature of the Hanbo incident while trying to cover up real power behind the scene," National Congress spokesman Yun Ho-jung told Reuters.
Kwon, who earlier said he would report to prosecutors on Tuesday, said he would now wait until prosecutors served him an official summons. Kwon was earlier summoned by telephone.

The National Congress and United Liberal Democrats, which together control 123 of 299 seats in parliament, have alleged government favouritism allowed Hanbo to expand its steelmaking flagship and acquire or set up 18 firms in the past three years.
